quote: Refeeding syndrome — start low, go slow, watch phosphate, give thiamine.
problem: The overlay card still teaches blanket 'start low, go slow' refeeding, while the page prose (remediated after prior finding MS3V04-F002) now correctly says current guidance favours higher-calorie refeeding with electrolyte surveillance over prolonged underfeeding. Overlay and prose contradict each other.
whyItMatters: A learner reading the stripped card will advocate conservative low-calorie starts for all malnourished patients, prolonging underfeeding (itself harmful, with longer admissions) contrary to SAHM 2022 guidance and the page's own text.
evidence: SAHM position paper 2022 (J Adolesc Health) — higher-calorie refeeding is safe in mild–moderate malnutrition with electrolyte monitoring; StRONG trial (Garber et al., JAMA Pediatr 2021); RCPsych MEED 2022. Page prose on this same page: 'The safe posture is close monitoring, not prolonged underfeeding'. Residue of prior finding MS3V04-F002 (prose fixed, overlay not).
correction: Refeeding syndrome — refeed per protocol with close electrolyte surveillance rather than prolonged underfeeding; watch phosphate, give thiamine.
verified: recall; prose on same page cross-checked

quote: **Refeeding syndrome = watch the phosphate** — start low, go slow, replete phosphate, give thiamine; the most malnourished are the highest risk.
problem: The high-yield pearl repeats 'start low, go slow' as the refeeding rule, contradicting the page's own refeeding section, which says current guidance supports higher-calorie refeeding with electrolyte surveillance and reserves the most conservative starts for the most severely malnourished.
whyItMatters: Pearls are what learners memorise; this one reinstates the superseded blanket-underfeeding teaching the prose was corrected to remove.
evidence: SAHM 2022 refeeding position paper; StRONG trial (Garber et al., JAMA Pediatr 2021); RCPsych MEED 2022; same page's refeeding paragraph.
correction: **Refeeding syndrome = watch the phosphate** — refeed per protocol with close electrolyte monitoring (conservative starts only for the most severely malnourished), replete phosphate, give thiamine; the most malnourished are the highest risk.
verified: recall; prose on same page cross-checked

quote: **olanzapine** may modestly help weight and obsessionality in AN
problem: The key RCT (Attia et al., Am J Psychiatry 2019) found a modest BMI benefit for olanzapine but no significant difference versus placebo in obsessionality (YBOCS obsessions subscale), which was a co-primary outcome.
whyItMatters: A learner will believe olanzapine treats the obsessional/psychological core of AN and may recommend it on that basis; the trial found no psychological benefit.
evidence: Attia E et al. Olanzapine versus placebo in adult outpatients with anorexia nervosa: RCT. Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(6):449-456 (PMID 30654643, doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.2018.18101125): 'no significant difference between treatment groups in change in the YBOCS obsessions subscale ... modest therapeutic effect ... on weight ... but no significant benefit for psychological symptoms.'
correction: **olanzapine** may modestly help weight (but not obsessionality) in AN

quote: aligned with APA, the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine (SAHM), and MARSIPAN medical-instability guidance
problem: The page's source line claims alignment with MARSIPAN, which the page's own refeeding section correctly says was replaced by MEED in 2022.
whyItMatters: Learners and adopting programmes are pointed to superseded guidance; the page contradicts its own citation.
evidence: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233, Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders (MEED), May 2022 — replaces MARSIPAN and Junior MARSIPAN.
correction: aligned with APA, the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine (SAHM), and MEED (RCPsych 2022, which replaced MARSIPAN) medical-instability guidance

quote: Postpartum psychosis typically appears in the first 1–4 weeks, recurs in 30–50% of subsequent deliveries, and is bipolar-spectrum until proven otherwise — screen for prior mania.
problem: The card's unsourced 30–50% recurrence figure conflicts with the page's own evidence-backed pearl (~29% severe recurrence after a prior postpartum psychosis, per the cited Wesseloo 2016 meta-analysis) and with the page's statement that data are insufficient to quote a figure for bipolar-plus-prior-episode.
whyItMatters: Learners see two different recurrence numbers for the same counselling question, and the card's figure is not what the linked evidence source reports.
evidence: Wesseloo R et al., Am J Psychiatry 2016;173:117-127 (PMID 26514657): severe postpartum episodes in 29% (95% CI 20–41) of women with a history of postpartum psychosis; overall high-risk relapse 35%; insufficient data for bipolar + prior postpartum episode. Page pearl on this surface quotes the same ~29%.
correction: Postpartum psychosis typically appears in the first 1–4 weeks, recurs as a severe episode after roughly 29% of subsequent deliveries in women with a prior episode, and is bipolar-spectrum until proven otherwise — screen for prior mania.

quote: for postpartum depression specifically, zuranolone is an oral option.
problem: Zuranolone is introduced with no mention of its boxed warning (CNS-depressant effects impairing driving; patients must not drive or do hazardous activities for at least 12 hours after each dose) or its fixed 14-day course.
whyItMatters: The patient population is new mothers who often drive with an infant; a learner who counsels or documents zuranolone without the driving restriction omits the label's central safety instruction.
evidence: Zurzuvae (zuranolone) US prescribing information, FDA approval Aug 2023 — BOXED WARNING: impaired ability to drive or engage in other potentially hazardous activities; advise not to drive for at least 12 hours after administration; 14-day course taken in the evening with fat-containing food.
correction: for postpartum depression specifically, zuranolone is an oral 14-day option (boxed warning: CNS depression — no driving or other hazardous activity for at least 12 hours after each dose).

quote: Effortful 'I don't know' answers with disengagement suggest pseudodementia — treat the depression and cognition improves.
problem: The card promises that cognition improves once the depression is treated. Late-life depression with cognitive impairment often does not fully resolve and carries a high risk of later dementia, so this is taught as reassurance rather than a reason for follow-up. The quiz option on the same page says 'treat the depression and retest cognition', which is the safer framing.
whyItMatters: A learner may reassure the family and close the cognitive question when the mood lifts, missing an early neurodegenerative process that needs follow-up.
evidence: Alexopoulos GS et al., Am J Psychiatry 1993;150:1693-1699 — 'reversible dementia' of depression: about 43% developed irreversible dementia over roughly 3 years, vs about 12% of depressed patients without cognitive impairment; the association between late-life depression and later dementia is repeatedly replicated.
correction: Effortful 'I don't know' answers with disengagement suggest pseudodementia — treat the depression and retest cognition; follow it after remission, because depression with cognitive impairment often precedes dementia.

quote: ADHD, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and intellectual disability (ID) — are usually the *context*
problem: DSM-5-TR renamed the diagnosis 'intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability)'. The page, including its exam-anchor table, uses only the DSM-5 (2013) label.
whyItMatters: Shelf items and current documentation use the DSM-5-TR name; learners will not recognise it as the same diagnosis.
evidence: DSM-5-TR (APA 2022), Neurodevelopmental Disorders: 'Intellectual Developmental Disorder (Intellectual Disability)'.
correction: ADHD, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability, ID) — are usually the *context*

quote: risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved for *irritability/aggression associated with autism*
problem: Both FDA approvals are for irritability associated with autistic disorder in children and adolescents only: risperidone ages 5–16, aripiprazole ages 6–17. On an adult unit, where this page and its first-move card recommend them, use is off-label.
whyItMatters: Residents will document and consent adult patients as though the drug has an on-label indication. That misstates the evidence base and the consent conversation for adults.
evidence: Risperdal PI (irritability associated with autistic disorder, ages 5–16, 2006); Abilify PI (ages 6–17, 2009).
correction: risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved for *irritability associated with autism* in children and adolescents (use in autistic adults is off-label)

quote: Social-communication deficits plus restricted/repetitive behaviors, insistence on sameness, or restricted interests from early development
problem: The row implies any single restricted or repetitive feature is enough. DSM-5-TR ASD requires deficits in all three social-communication areas (A1–A3) plus at least two of the four restricted/repetitive patterns (B1–B4), and B4 is sensory hyper- or hyporeactivity, which the row leaves out.
whyItMatters: The row is labelled a shelf discriminator, so a learner would apply a criterion threshold that is too low.
evidence: DSM-5-TR (2022) Autism Spectrum Disorder, Criteria A (all 3 of A1–A3) and B (at least 2 of B1–B4, including sensory hyper/hyporeactivity).
correction: Deficits in all three social-communication areas plus at least two of four restricted/repetitive patterns (stereotyped behavior or speech, insistence on sameness, restricted interests, sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity), present from early development

quote: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis** — use the lowest dose for the shortest time
problem: The BPSD section says nothing about brexpiprazole, the only FDA-approved drug for agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer disease (May 2023), or that the class boxed warning still applies to it.
whyItMatters: Residents will not know an on-label option exists. They may also read the 2023 approval, if they meet it elsewhere, as lifting the mortality warning, which it does not.
evidence: FDA approval of Rexulti (brexpiprazole) supplemental indication, 10 May 2023: agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer's disease; label retains the boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
correction: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis** (it applies equally to brexpiprazole, FDA-approved in 2023 for agitation associated with Alzheimer dementia) — use the lowest dose for the shortest time

quote: - Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild–moderate; add memantine for moderate–severe.
problem: Donepezil is FDA-approved for severe as well as mild and moderate Alzheimer dementia, and so is the high-dose rivastigmine patch. The pearl suggests cholinesterase inhibitors stop at moderate disease.
whyItMatters: Learners may stop or withhold a cholinesterase inhibitor in severe disease, where it remains an approved option, usually alongside memantine.
evidence: Aricept (donepezil) PI — indicated for mild, moderate and severe dementia of the Alzheimer's type (severe-stage approval 2006); Exelon Patch PI (severe AD, 2013).
correction: - Cholinesterase inhibitors from mild disease onward (donepezil is approved through severe AD); add memantine for moderate–severe.

quote: a delirium is layered on a dementia far more often than either occurs alone
problem: This comparative claim has no source and is doubtful as written: dementia without delirium is far more common than delirium superimposed on dementia. The defensible point is that dementia is the strongest predisposing factor for delirium, and that delirium superimposed on dementia is common in hospitalised older adults.
whyItMatters: The statement is not literally true, and a learner may repeat it as fact.
evidence: Fick DM et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2002 (systematic review; delirium superimposed on dementia prevalence 22–89% in hospital/community samples); Inouye SK et al., Lancet 2014 (dementia as leading predisposing factor for delirium).
correction: dementia is the strongest predisposing factor for delirium, and delirium superimposed on dementia is common in hospitalized older adults

quote: (a key DSM-5-TR shift from "medically unexplained")
problem: The move from 'medically unexplained' symptoms (DSM-IV somatization and somatoform disorders) to somatic symptom disorder happened in DSM-5 (2013), not in DSM-5-TR (2022).
whyItMatters: This is a minor factual error about the history of the classification.
evidence: DSM-5 (APA 2013) introduced Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders; DSM-5-TR (2022) text revision retained it.
correction: (a key DSM-5 shift, retained in DSM-5-TR, from "medically unexplained")

quote: *Not a mental disorder* — a V-code/observation.
problem: V-codes were the ICD-9-CM codes for 'other conditions that may be a focus of clinical attention'. DSM-5-TR lists these conditions with ICD-10-CM Z-codes only, and malingering is Z76.5.
whyItMatters: Learners will use a coding term that has not been current since 2015.
evidence: DSM-5-TR (2022), Other Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention — Malingering, Z76.5; US transition to ICD-10-CM 1 Oct 2015.
correction: *Not a mental disorder* — a Z-code (Z76.5) condition that may be a focus of clinical attention.

quote: iron repletion and dopaminergic/alpha-2-delta agents for restless legs
problem: The page lists dopaminergic agents alongside alpha-2-delta ligands for RLS. The 2024 AASM guideline strongly recommends alpha-2-delta ligands and iron, and conditionally recommends against standard use of pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine because of augmentation.
whyItMatters: A learner would treat dopamine agonists as an equal first choice, which puts patients at risk of augmentation (worsening, earlier-onset RLS), the reason the guideline moved away from them.
evidence: Winkelman JW et al., Treatment of restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder: an AASM clinical practice guideline, J Clin Sleep Med 2025;21(1):137-152 (released 2024) — strong for gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, pregabalin, IV ferric carboxymaltose; conditional against standard use of pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine.
correction: iron repletion and alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) for restless legs — the 2024 AASM guideline advises against standard use of dopamine agonists because of augmentation

quote: Paraphilic disorders involving a child or non-consenting person raise safety and reporting duties.
problem: The card treats a non-consenting adult victim (exhibitionism, voyeurism, frotteurism) as creating a clinician reporting duty. US mandatory reporting covers child abuse and, depending on the state, elder or dependent-adult abuse. A patient's disclosure of past offences against competent adults is ordinarily confidential, and a breach is justified only under the state's duty-to-warn or duty-to-protect law for a credible threat to an identifiable person. That law is mandatory, permissive or absent depending on the state.
whyItMatters: A learner could breach confidentiality, and HIPAA, by 'reporting' disclosed paraphilic behaviour against adults, or could miss that the real trigger is a threat to an identifiable person under their state's law.
evidence: State mandatory-reporting statutes (child abuse universal; elder/dependent-adult abuse by state); Tarasoff v Regents (Cal 1976) and state duty-to-protect statutes (mandatory/permissive/none); HIPAA 45 CFR 164.512(j) (serious and imminent threat).
correction: Paraphilic disorders involving a child raise child-protection reporting duties; with non-consenting adults, confidentiality holds unless your state's duty-to-protect law is triggered by a credible threat to an identifiable person.

quote: - Non-consenting paraphilic behavior triggers safety and reporting duties.
problem: This pearl is broader than the law: non-consenting paraphilic behaviour toward adults does not generally trigger a clinician reporting duty. The page's 'Can't-miss' paragraph and the student bullet ('when a paraphilic disorder involves a child or non-consenting person') have the same problem, but the page elsewhere correctly limits child-protection reporting to cases where a child is at risk.
whyItMatters: A learner could breach confidentiality over a disclosure that no statute requires reporting.
evidence: As for the overlay finding: state child/elder-abuse reporting statutes; state duty-to-protect laws (mandatory/permissive/none); HIPAA 45 CFR 164.512(j).
correction: - A child at risk triggers child-protection reporting; other non-consenting paraphilic behavior triggers a safety assessment and, only for a credible threat to an identifiable person, your state's duty-to-protect rules.

quote: confirm criteria for other disorders aren't met, quantify suicide risk, and start brief supportive therapy.
problem: 'Quantify suicide risk' asks the learner to put a number or level on risk. Current practice, and this curriculum's own stance, is structured assessment and formulation with a safety plan, not an actuarial risk level; risk scales and categories predict poorly.
whyItMatters: On a card shown without the page's hedging, a learner may assign a 'low risk' label to a 'subthreshold' adjustment presentation and treat it as licence for disposition. That is the failure the page's can't-miss line warns about.
evidence: NICE NG225 (2022) Self-harm, rec 1.5.x — do not use risk tools/scales to predict future suicide or to determine who should or should not be offered treatment or be discharged; Large M et al. meta-analyses of risk categorisation (e.g., PLoS One 2016); Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01.
correction: confirm criteria for other disorders aren't met, assess and formulate suicide risk directly (no risk-level label), and start brief supportive therapy.

quote: - Screen and *quantify* suicide risk — don't be lulled by "mild."
problem: The student action explicitly tells the learner to quantify suicide risk. That points toward actuarial levels rather than an assessment, a formulation and a safety plan.
whyItMatters: Learners may record a numeric or categorical risk level as the output of the assessment and base disposition on it.
evidence: NICE NG225 (2022) — do not use risk scales or categorisation to determine management or discharge; Stanley–Brown safety planning as the intervention.
correction: - Assess suicide risk directly and formulate it (drivers, protective factors, safety plan) — don't be lulled by "mild."

quote: Set up the psychosocial interventions (parent training, MST, skills therapy), continuity for ADHD/mood/substance treatment, and a safety plan.
problem: The page asks learners to assess violence and suicide risk and victim safety, and it ends with a discharge safety plan, but it has not opted in to the build-injected crisis-contacts block. Adjustment, dissociative, eating and perinatal pages that do comparable risk work have opted in.
whyItMatters: The discharge safety plan the page tells learners to write has no crisis contacts attached on this page. Under the library's own crisis-block policy, that is a gap for a page doing disposition risk work.
evidence: Library crisis-block policy (CLAUDE.md: a page where the learner plausibly does risk assessment or disposition should carry the <!-- crisis-block --> marker); this page's 'Assess violence and suicide risk and victim safety' workup line.
correction: Set up the psychosocial interventions (parent training, MST, skills therapy), continuity for ADHD/mood/substance treatment, and a safety plan with crisis contacts (see below). <!-- crisis-block -->
